THE ORACLE RELIABILITY LAB

More regions.
More chances to be wrong.

Keep a hypothetical detector's quality fixed, then grow the search from 16 to 64 regions. A small false-positive rate can spread amplified probability across the wrong places.

This is an exact calculation for a constructed independent-error model. These rates are controls you choose, not measured QNN accuracy or predictions about your images.

True-target probabilityAccepted-set probability

Each nonempty oracle uses its known marked count to select the first Grover peak. Empty oracles abstain and contribute zero effective output probability. Means include all constructed cases, including abstentions.

WHY THE NUMBERS SEPARATE

Confidence follows
the accepted set.

For t true regions among N, let A be accepted true regions and B accepted false regions. Their independent binomial distributions define the possible predicates. The calculation averages the exact Grover result for every count pair.

A ~ Bin(t, recall)
B ~ Bin(N − t, false-positive rate)
P(any false mark) = 1 − (1 − f)N − t

Every true region counts.

A true region that the detector rejects can retain some unmarked Born probability when the oracle is nonempty. The calculation includes that residual mass; it does not assume true success is always accepted probability divided by the number of marks.

Count the work before search.

The current image demos evaluate every candidate classically: 16 or 64 detector calls. Fewer ideal Grover oracle calls do not remove that compilation work. Gate decomposition, image loading, coherent data access and wall time are not estimated here.

A comparison without a speedup claim.

The calculation also reports uniformly selecting an accepted region as a classical reference. Binary marks alone cannot predict a score-based argmax. Neither reference establishes a practical quantum advantage.

Inspect the exact target formula ↓

For 0 < M < N, with M = A + B and PG the Grover accepted-set probability:

P(true | A,B) = (A/M)PG + ((t − A)/(N − M))(1 − PG)

For M = 0 the application abstains. For M = N the distribution is uniform and true probability is t/N. Averaging uses the probability weight of every A,B pair, not one typical marked count. The round choice knows M for each predicate; it is not an unknown-target-count search algorithm.
